podcast.title: Band Name Origin
podcast.body: The name "Alexis on Fire" originated from a Discovery Channel segment about a contortionist stripper named Alexis Fire, where the segment itself was titled "Alexis on fire." The band members quickly adopted it, not expecting their band to gain widespread recognition. They later received and ignored cease and desist letters regarding the name and deliberately chose to write it as one word, which often led to mispronunciations like "Alex's on fire." "And in one of the segments, they did a segment on a girl who's a stripper, who was also a contortionist, and she amongst other things, which we would come to find out. But her name was Alexis Fire and the segment was called Alexis on fire."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alexisonfire - In Their Own Words Podcast

podcast.title: Connoisseurship vs. Consumption
podcast.body: The band's rise occurred in an era where music connoisseurship was more prevalent than instant consumption. Before streaming and widespread internet access, fans had to actively seek out music by attending shows, knowing people, or acquiring physical records. This created a deeper investment in the music that resonated with them. "But it's more about connoisseurship than it is consumption. Because back then before streaming before, you know, the internet, you had to seek out this stuff."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alexisonfire - In Their Own Words Podcast

podcast.title: Dallas Green's Departure
podcast.body: Dallas Green decided to leave the band not for solo success, but due to creative differences, feeling he could no longer write aggressive music and did not want to force it. He attempted to continue both Alexis on Fire and City and Colour but found he couldn't write aggressive material naturally anymore. The breakup was amicable, and it was acknowledged that he "probably should have left Alexis on Fire four years earlier" as City and Colour had begun to eclipse Alexis on Fire in popularity. "I left the band solely because I had creatively I wanted to do something else."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alexisonfire - In Their Own Words Podcast

podcast.title: Early Career Aspirations
podcast.body: The band initially had modest aspirations, not expecting mainstream success or radio play. Their highest goal was to play to about 200 people at venues like The Cathedral in downtown Toronto, believing their type of music would lead to obscurity. "The top of the, the top of the heap would have been playing to 200 people at the cathedral downtown Toronto. Yeah. That was as big as the aspirations."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alexisonfire - In Their Own Words Podcast

podcast.title: Early Niagara Music Scene
podcast.body: The band members met by playing in various other local bands around Niagara, southern Ontario. The scene was characterized by "incestuous sort of stuff" with musicians frequently moving between groups. Shows were often kid-promoted in 200- or 150-capacity clubs, or rented halls like Columbus Hall, Masonic temples, and Canadian Auto Workers Union Halls for a couple hundred bucks. Bands would sometimes play at places like the Kingwalk Court, a Chinese food restaurant in St. Catharines, and be paid in beer, which was beneficial given their underage status. "A lot of kid promoted shows. Like people who are like in high school, they rent out a... A pole, a shop. A pole, a shop. Nice Columbus Hall, Masonic temples, Canadian auto workers union hall."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alexisonfire - In Their Own Words Podcast

podcast.title: MuchMusic Impact
podcast.body: MuchMusic played a crucial role in Alexis on Fire's rise to prominence. Managers Joel and Trisha, label head Greg, and EMI's Michael, along with George Stroumboulopoulos (who wore their t-shirt and brought them on MuchMusic before they had recorded anything), championed the band. MuchMusic's ability to connect listeners across Canada, from St. John's to Yellowknife, allowed their music to resonate with a wider audience who felt a connection to their sound. "Much music back in the day is that it linked a kid in St. John's Newfoundland with a kid in Yellowknife. And you could turn it on and see an Alexis on Fire video and go, that sounds like I feel."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alexisonfire - In Their Own Words Podcast

podcast.title: Pop Music Shift
podcast.body: The rise of Alexis on Fire and similar aggressive bands coincided with a shift in pop music in the mid-2000s. Fans who had grown up with pop acts like Backstreet Boys, N'Sync, Christina Aguilera, and Britney Spears from the mid-90s were aging and seeking music that expressed anger, fears, and frustrations, creating an opening for bands like Alexis on Fire and Billy Talent. "But during that time, we were seeing the end of the spike in pop music, you know, the back street boys and instincts and Christine Aguilar is in Britney Spears and that group of people who had been into pop since the middle 90s with spice girls and whatever, they were now getting older and they were getting angry and they were looking for something that spoke to that anger and their fears and their frustrations."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alexisonfire - In Their Own Words Podcast

podcast.title: Post-Breakup Lives
podcast.body: Following the band's breakup, members pursued different paths: Dallas Green continued with City and Colour, George Pettit became a firefighter, Wade McNeil became a radio DJ, Jordan Hastings became a fill-in drummer for Billy Talent and played in other bands, and Chris Steele was last heard to have gone for a "truck on the Himalayas." "I mean, Dallas Green is off doing a city and color thing. Vocalist George Pettit became a firefighter. Wade McNeil is doing a bunch of stuff, including working as a radio DJ. Drummer Jordan Hastings is filling it with Billy Talbot and playing in some other bands. And I'm not even sure where bass player Chris Steele is."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alexisonfire - In Their Own Words Podcast

podcast.title: Post-Crisis Plateau
podcast.body: While "Old Crows / Young Cardinals" was successful, it was perceived as a step down from the monumental success of "Crisis" and did not reach number one. This marked the first time the band saw a drop in ticket sales in some locations, leading to a feeling that they had hit a ceiling and caused doubts among the members after years of consistent progress. "And as much as it was a success, it was a step down from crisis. And I think that, in some way, it just, I think until that point, it was just step up, after step up, after step up, like we were always making a little bit of progress."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alexisonfire - In Their Own Words Podcast

podcast.title: Resilience and Delivery
podcast.body: The band members emphasized their resilience and commitment to "deliver" whenever given an opportunity. They never "botched anything," successfully performing at major events like the MuchMusic Video Awards, despite the pressure of a gigantic stage. "I will say this in full humble, in full humbleness, Alexis on Fire f*** delivers. When it comes down to like the moment, like if we need to do something, don't people draw a drawing that please."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alexisonfire - In Their Own Words Podcast

podcast.title: Reunion Motivation
podcast.body: The reunion was driven by the members remaining close, enjoying playing together, and sensing strong public demand. They initially played sporadic shows as a "vacation," but Dallas Green's move back to Toronto led to more regular practices and the decision to write new music, rather than just playing old hits. Despite the challenges of balancing music with family life and other aspirations, the "neural pathway" carved through years of playing live made returning feel natural and joyful. "It just became, it became no excuse for us to not play. Yeah. That's really what it was."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alexisonfire - In Their Own Words Podcast

podcast.title: Right Place, Right Time
podcast.body: The band attributed much of their success to a combination of luck and seizing opportunities at the right moment. They acknowledge that many equally talented bands fall by the wayside or never achieve the same level of recognition, often due to not being in the "right exact spot at the right exact time." They also noted a tendency in Canadian culture to promote "palatable" music over potentially "best" cultural output. "We just happened to be the band that got that video and got, we had a bunch of open doors and yeah, in the right time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alexisonfire - In Their Own Words Podcast

podcast.title: Successful Canadian Indy Band
podcast.body: Alexis On Fire is recognized as one of the best-selling Canadian Indy bands in recent years. They record for the Indy label Distort, which, due to lacking its own comprehensive distribution capabilities, subcontracts all its distribution needs to the major label Universal. This partnership allows them to maintain their independent status while benefiting from broader market reach. "This is how Alexis On Fire managed to become one of the best selling Canadian Indy bands the last few years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Etymology: Part 1

podcast.title: The Breakup's Positive Impact
podcast.body: The band members ultimately view their breakup as a positive development, allowing each individual to pursue other aspects of their lives and careers without growing to resent each other. It prevented the band from reaching a point where they were "at each other's throats" and ultimately enabled their reunion under better circumstances. "No, the dust is settled too. I mean like the breakup was the best thing to happen to all of us. It really was."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alexisonfire - In Their Own Words Podcast

podcast.title: Touring Challenges
podcast.body: The band experienced significant disparity in audience numbers during their early tours. For example, they played a successful show at the Croatian Cultural Center in Vancouver to a thousand people with Billy Talent, only to cross the border into Bellingham, Washington, and play for only the bar staff, with Dallas Green not even performing due to voice issues. Later, attempts to "hammer it" in America during the "Old Crows" era, including a "disastrous" Warped Tour and long unfulfilling American tours where only 40-60% of shows were good, became mentally exhausting. "We played for the bar staff. I don't even think I played the show. You didn't. I didn't. I took a T-shirt. Because your voice was bothering you."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alexisonfire - In Their Own Words Podcast

podcast.title: Wade McNeil's Promotion Skills
podcast.body: Even at 15 years old, Wade McNeil was adept at negotiating and promoting shows. He was known for organizing events and was responsible for booking Alexis on Fire's first American tour by connecting with people in internet chat rooms. "Wade was one of those kids. Wade can promote a show. Wade at 15 years old is Negoshi."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alexisonfire - In Their Own Words Podcast

podcast.title: Watch Out Album Artwork
podcast.body: The artwork for the "Watch Out" album features two Catholic schoolgirls engaged in a knife fight. This imagery was inspired by a long-standing joke where the band would describe their sound on flyers as "two Catholic schoolgirls in a knife fight." Dallas Green photographed his then-girlfriend and her friend, who were actual Catholic high school students at the time and wore their own school uniforms for the shoot. "So when you make flyers for a show, back in the day you'd always have like the name of the band and then underneath it in parentheses or whatever, we'd have a little description of what the band was. And it was always something like, you know, crushing buffalo metal core or like, you know, whatever."

xref.title: Early 2010s Decline and Mid-2010s Return
xref.body: Alexisonfire "went away" in the early 2010s as emo began to wane, with fans growing up and bands breaking up. However, they returned by the middle of the decade, signaling a strong emo revival alongside a new generation of groups exploring the genre. "Alexis on Fire went away." "Alexis on Fire returned."

xref.title: Early Canadian Tour
xref.body: Billy Talent toured across Canada with Alexis on Fire and Death from Above around 2002-2003, during the period of Alexis on Fire's first record. This tour allowed both bands to see a country-wide audience of 500-600 capacity venues. "We went across Canada with death from above. And that was, yeah, that was where we got to see it every night, you know, because we had only played Southern Ontario really."

xref.title: Genre Blending and Influence
xref.body: NoMeansNo occupied a unique space by blending elements of hardcore and metal. Their sound contained elements that would later define post-hardcore, influencing bands like At the Drive-In, Rollins Band, Alexisonfire, Billy Talent, Deftones, and Silverstein. "They ended up occupying a space somewhere between hardcore and metal. If you listen carefully to what they did, you can hear elements of what would become known as post-hardcore, a sound that would later birth groups like at the drive-in, Rollins Band, Alexis on Fire, Billy Talent, The Death Tones and Silverstein."

xref.body: Alexisonfire originated in St. Catharines, Canada, and became one of the most significant bands in the Screamo genre, achieving multiple Gold and Platinum albums in Canada and reaching number one on the National Album charts multiple times. Their international fanbase grew to include the US, Australia, and the UK. "the other was Alexis On Fire, which was born down the highway in St. Catharines."

xref.title: Shared Influence
xref.body: Converge was a band that all members of Alexis on Fire "kind of came together" on as an influence. George Pettit and Dallas Green even met Liam from Cancer Bats at a Converge show, indicating its significance in their formative musical experiences. "Converge, I think we all kind of came together."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alexisonfire - In Their Own Words Podcast

xref.title: Shared Rise to Prominence
xref.body: Billy Talent and Alexis on Fire experienced a similar breakthrough around the same time, with both bands gaining opportunities and radio attention with songs like "Pulmonary Archery" and "Try Honesty." They shared a Canadian tour alongside Death from Above, playing larger venues and witnessing the demand for aggressive music across the country. "And I think when the, when Palm and I started getting played across Canada, it was the same time Billy Talent and Tri-Honesty started clicking and they started getting radio attention as well."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alexisonfire - In Their Own Words Podcast

xref.title: Successful Canadian Indy Band
xref.body: Alexis On Fire is recognized as one of the best-selling Canadian Indy bands in recent years. They record for the Indy label Distort, which, due to lacking its own comprehensive distribution capabilities, subcontracts all its distribution needs to the major label Universal. This partnership allows them to maintain their independent status while benefiting from broader market reach. "This is how Alexis On Fire managed to become one of the best selling Canadian Indy bands the last few years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Etymology: Part 1

xref.title: Third Wave Emo Chart Success
xref.body: Alexisonfire was among the bands whose emo records achieved mainstream success during the third wave of emo (early 2000s), with their albums reaching the top 10 on charts. "Emo records from bands like...Alexis on Fire... all rocketed into the top 10 on the album charts."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 3: Emo

xref.title: Touring Before Stardom
xref.body: Alexis on Fire toured with Avenged Sevenfold right before Avenged Sevenfold signed their major label deals and released the records that would launch them into superstardom. This tour offered a glimpse into the major label courting process and the impending surge in popularity for aggressive music. "I remember we did a, we did a long American tour with, it was us, Mike him and Evan Sevenfold, both right before both those, like both of them have just signed their major label deals and both had made the records that would then propel them into super stardom, but it was the tour right before that."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alexisonfire - In Their Own Words Podcast

xref.title: Wade McNeil's Promotion Skills
xref.body: Even at 15 years old, Wade McNeil was adept at negotiating and promoting shows. He was known for organizing events and was responsible for booking Alexis on Fire's first American tour by connecting with people in internet chat rooms. "Wade was one of those kids. Wade can promote a show. Wade at 15 years old is Negoshi."
